In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmet: don't return memory contents beyond valid data when reading ANA log page

The host side does not know how much valid data will be returned by the target
so it will typically provide a buffer larger than the amount of valid data in
the ANA log page.  The memory allocation used by the target does not guarantee
that prior kernel memory contents will not be returned past the end of the valid
page data.  Fix this to ensure that the SGL is zeroed before copying the data.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: line6: Reject capture buffers smaller than two packets

line6_capture_copy() splits the copy into the ALSA ring buffer once at
the buffer end and wraps pos_done once, which is only correct when one
packet holds at most buffer_size frames. The packet size comes from the
device's endpoint, and the per-device hw structs allow 64-byte periods
with periods_min 1, so a packet can be larger than the whole buffer.
audio_in_callback() logs an oversized packet and then copies it anyway.

The packet size is known at probe time, so constrain
SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_BYTES in snd_line6_capture_open() to at least
twice the larger of the two endpoints' packet sizes. Two rather than
one, because pos_done advances by the packet and wraps once, so a buffer
of exactly one packet leaves the position unchanged after every packet.
hw_params then rejects a buffer that cannot hold two packets, and the
single wrap is valid for every configuration that gets through. Keep a
guard in line6_capture_copy() that drops an oversized packet with a
ratelimited error, for the case that should no longer be reachable.

Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the GuitarPort
interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 128-byte buffer: ALSA
logged "invalid position: pos = 224, buffer size = 32" and the driver
logged "driver bug: len" on every following packet. With this patch a
1024-byte buffer is refused at hw_params, and a 2048-byte buffer streams
for 30 s with no report and with the position moving inside the buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: usx2y: Require a buffer of two URBs

usx2y_urb_capt_retire() wraps the ring buffer once per packet and
usx2y_urb_play_prepare() once per URB of nr_of_packs() packets of up to
50 frames. Both assume that the data fits in the buffer, and the hw
constraints only require about two 1 ms periods, so a packet larger
than the buffer on capture, or a URB larger than the buffer on playback,
violates that assumption.

Constrain SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_SIZE in snd_usx2y_pcm_open() to at
least two URBs, 2 * nr_of_packs() * 50 frames, for both directions. The
bound is in frames and derived from the driver's own packet limit, so it
does not read the endpoint, whose altsetting is only selected in
prepare. Two URBs rather than one, because the position advances by a
URB on playback and only moves when a URB is less than the whole buffer.
Keep a guard in usx2y_urb_capt_retire() that drops a packet larger than
the buffer, for the case the constraint makes unreachable.

With nrpacks above about 163 (S16_LE) or 109 (S24_3LE) the bound exceeds
the 64 KiB buffer the substream preallocates (twice that with the
preallocation raised to its 128 KiB maximum), so hw_params fails for
those module settings. That is intended: the driver cannot be safe with
a URB larger than half the largest buffer.

Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the US-122
interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 512-byte capture buffer:

  BUG: KASAN: out-of-bounds in i_usx2y_urb_complete+0x1285/0x1ac0
  Read of size 18446744073709551104 at addr ffff88800e448800 by task vhci_rx/83

Tested on 7.3-rc7 with the same device, S16_LE at 44100 Hz, nrpacks 4,
so the bound is 400 frames. A 128-frame capture buffer and a 200-frame
playback buffer are refused at hw_params with EINVAL. A 400-frame buffer
streams for 30 s in each direction with the position advancing inside
the buffer and no KASAN report; the capture guard did not fire. The
same 400-frame capture buffer with S24_3LE, which selects altsetting 2
in prepare, streams for 30 s with the same result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners

mptcp_pm_nl_create_listen_socket() starts the TCP listener directly
instead of going through mptcp_listen(). It consequently misses setting
SOCK_RCU_FREE on the parent MPTCP socket.

tcp_child_process() can invoke the listener's subflow_data_ready()
callback without holding the MPTCP parent lock or a reference to the
parent. An authenticated MP_JOIN racing with endpoint teardown can
therefore access the parent after its last reference has been dropped.
The ADD_ADDR error path can also close an already published listener.

Set SOCK_RCU_FREE before __inet_listen_sk() publishes the TCP listener,
matching mptcp_listen(). This protects the parent on every subsequent
close path, including a failed endpoint addition.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: don't let the extent type hide an exhausted free-space table extent

udf_table_new_block() takes the first block of the free-space table
extent closest to the goal.  It keeps that extent's type and length
together in goal_elen, subtracts one block, and deletes the extent only
if goal_elen then reaches zero.  UDF 2.60 section 2.3.7.1 requires the
free-space extents of an Unallocated Space Entry to be of type 1
(allocated but not recorded), and mkudffs writes them that way.  For
such an extent the type bits keep goal_elen non-zero, so taking its last
block leaves a type-1 extent of length zero behind, starting at the
block after the extent, which is in use.

The next allocation that picks this empty extent returns that in-use
block.  Subtracting a block from 0x40000000 then borrows from the type
bits, and the extent becomes type 0 with a length of 2^30 - blocksize:
about a gigabyte of "free" space overlapping live metadata, the other
table extents and whatever lies behind the partition.  From then on
blocks are handed out twice, or past the end of the partition.

Extents that udf_table_free_blocks() adds are type 0, where the check
works, so only tables written by mkudffs or by another implementation
are affected.  Nothing more than filling such a filesystem is needed:
on a fresh 1 MiB "mkudffs --space=unalloctable" image, creating empty
files until the partition is full writes file entries over the reserve
volume descriptor sequence and the backup anchor, and df then reports a
negative amount of used space.

On syzbot's images the same double allocation is what the two reports
below trip over.  In the first, ftruncate() extends a new file with
enough hole extents to need a chain of allocation extent descriptors;
one AED is placed on another inode's file entry, and a later one is
placed on the block of the AED currently being filled, which
udf_setup_indirect_aext() zeroes, so __udf_add_aext() finds
lengthAllocDescs out of step with its cursor.  In the second, an AED
is placed past the end of the device, sb_getblk() fails, and the error
path of udf_do_extend_file() calls udf_truncate_extents() on an extent
list that no longer covers i_size.

Keep the type separately from the length, as udf_table_prealloc_blocks()
already does.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: check the unallocated space table when it is loaded

udf_table_new_block() hands out the first block of the extent closest
to its goal and trusts that the extent covers at least one whole block
inside the partition.  Nothing checks that.  A zero-length extent makes
it return the block the extent points at, which need not be free, and
the subtraction of one block then underflows the length into the type
bits, turning the entry into a bogus continuation.  An extent running
past the end of the partition makes it return blocks behind the
partition.

Such tables are not only found on crafted images: until the previous
commit, udf_table_new_block() itself left zero-length extents behind
in tables written by mkudffs, and then converted them into extents
running past the partition.

Check every extent once when the table is loaded, and refuse
read-write access if one is empty, is not a whole number of blocks, or
does not lie inside the partition, in the same way as for other
allocation information the kernel cannot use.  Check first that the
table is an Unallocated Space Entry at all: the walk starts at the
offset of the allocation descriptors in one, and for a file entry that
offset lies before the inode's in-memory copy of the descriptors.
Treat a chain of allocation extent descriptors that leads back to
itself the same way: the walk would otherwise return the same extents
forever, and the mount would never finish.  Let a fatal signal
interrupt the walk and fail the mount.

Refusing read-write access to an empty extent is deliberate.  It shows
that an old kernel took the last block but left the entry behind.  If
consumed again, the entry returns an in-use block and turns into a huge
bogus extent.  Refusing the table before that
happens avoids this second allocation; the filesystem can still be
mounted read-only.  The check cannot detect every overlap that may
already exist in a damaged table.

This patch should be backported together with the previous one: that
patch stops creating new empty extents, and this one rejects existing
ones before they are consumed again.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes

On AMD CPUs with INVLPGB, two live processes can get the same MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE
global ASID value. The two then hit each other's TLB entries, so each can read
or corrupt the other's memory.

The global ASID space is managed lazily. When a global ASID is freed, its bit is
set in the global_asid_freed bitmap. Once the free ASID search reaches the end
of the global_asid_used bitmap, a global flush is done to really reclaim the
lazily freed global ASIDs.

However, the current code can assign the same global ASID to two different
processes, if one process is assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE - 1, another process
MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, and both stick around (keeping their global ASID numbers in
use) until the search wraps around again.  At that point a third process could
also get assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE.

    the highest ASID stays in use, so it is not handed out again
      last_global_asid stays below it, so no reset
        the clear bits run out
          find_next_zero_bit() returns MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE
            global_asid_available > 0, so the failure is not caught
              MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE is handed out as an ASID

A search only looks at the bits below MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, so it cannot see that
this value is in use. The next failed search hands it out again, even if the
first process still holds it.

The fix used here is to reset the global ASID space after a failed search, and
to search again. If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out.

The test for !global_asid_available is removed, because use_global_asid() only
calls allocate_global_asid() if global_asid_available > 0. The remaining test is
for a condition that should be impossible.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size

IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE)
that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table.
For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the
IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the
device table.

The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB
pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the
out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit
this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring
down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device
table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB.

Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected
processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a
(Zen5/BRH).

This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963.

kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size
encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches
pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched
kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB,
so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs
that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this
patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel
and the crash kernel together.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data()

The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the
client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need()
only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes.
ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio
with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more
inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end.

Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant()
and fill_inode(), are covered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client

When a ROAMING_ADV is received for an announced local client,
batadv_tt_local_mark_removed() sets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM, queues a
DEL|ROAM change and marks the entry as BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING. If the
client sends a frame again before the next TTVN commit,
batadv_tt_local_add_existing() only clears the PENDING flag and returns
early. The ADD cancels the queued DEL, but the entry keeps the ROAM flag:

* batadv_is_my_client() reports the client as not served by this node
* batadv_tt_local_client_is_roaming() reroutes unicast frames for it to
  the node which sent the ROAMING_ADV

The ROAM flag is only removed with the next frame of the client.

Since BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM is set together with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING,
it has to be cleared also at the same time with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING
when the client roamed back.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA

The erratum (MMU-700: #3777127, S3: #3673557) deals with under
invalidation of a CONT PTE grouping in the SMMU. The recommended work
around is to use a range invalidation that spans the entire CONT. The only
user of CONT in the kernel right now is through SVA sharing a CPU page
table that contains a CONT created by the mm.

Previously it was thought that this errata was dealt with because the
driver always uses range invalidation. However, there is a subtle detail
in the errata that the invalidation range must fully enclose the entire
CONT for it to work.

It seems that two sequential range invalidations, with a split point
falling inside a CONT grouping, will not prevent the errata.

The SMMU's range invalidation generation algorithm does not produce a
single invalidation for a single SVA invalidation request, nor does the mm
carefully align the SVA invalidation ranges to accommodate the splitting
of the invalidation into several ranges.

Thus, when processing a SVA invalidation, the range invalidation splitting
routine can generate a range invalidation that is split in the middle of
the CONT and risk under invalidation from this errata. This condition
could be triggered by a malicious userspace manipulating the TLB gathers
via mmap/mprotect/munmap.

Update the errata list to the include the S3 variation, detect the IOMMUs
that have it, and then have SVA invalidations use a simplified version of
the over invalidation algorithm from the tlbi rework series. This ensures
that a single range invalidation is issued for a single MMU notifier
callback and now the range invalidation is guarenteed to cover any posible
CONT.

Future work to add CONT to iommu_domain page tables should either use this
one-invalidate/one-range invalidation algorithm or disable CONT support in
the iommu_domain.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: hold shkey across socket migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the
new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops
the skb-owned shared-key reference.

If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the
final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the
freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference.

Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release
it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected
authentication key throughout the ownership transfer.

Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and
validated by Trail of Bits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained
control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can
therefore access the socket after it has been freed.

Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use
sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA
ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it
is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers.

Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration
so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings

find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that
are not CoW mappings, which is wrong.

If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have
VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE.

While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires
VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon()
still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma.

This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such
that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that
actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would
require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first
place.

copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared
PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are
shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function
with shareable page tables is the real issue.

If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it
might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant
locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and
possibly freed after calling:

	dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz);

To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a
safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never
end up messing with shared PMD tables in there.

Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd
operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an
anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma.

As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and
also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well
directly for consistency.

A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma)
lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of
VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on
CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack

sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy
lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone,
and nothing compares either length against that allocation.

sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which
added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties
each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the
allocation, which is the half this adds.

Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the
first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers,
so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is
enough; the filesystem does not have to be used.

Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches
differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small
overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync()

smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() waited for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED
after smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work() called rdma_disconnect(). That
can take very long, e.g. if the peer just disappeared, until the
rdma cm gives up, or forever if the event already happened, but the
status was overwritten afterwards.

This is not needed: smbdirect_socket_destroy() drains the qp under
rdma_lock_handler(), destroys it and calls rdma_destroy_id(), which
only waits for a currently running event handler and makes sure no
further events are delivered. The rest of the disconnect protocol
(DREQ/DREP and timewait for IB, abrupt close for iWarp) is handled
by the rdma core asynchronously. drivers/nvme/host/rdma.c also just
calls rdma_disconnect() and ib_drain_qp() before rdma_destroy_id().

So smbdirect_socket_destroy() now also accepts
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTING and changes the status to
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTED itself under rdma_lock_handler().

We could still get RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in the small
windows between rdma_unlock_handler() and rdma_destroy_id(),
but in that case smbdirect_connection_rdma_event_handler()
is basically a no-op.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener

A child of a listener only left the listen.pending or listen.ready
list via smbdirect_socket_accept() or when the listener was
destroyed. So every connection that failed before it was accepted
(negotiate timeout, peer disconnect, invalid negotiate request, ...)
stayed on the list and counted against the backlog until the listener
was destroyed. After about backlog (10 for ksmbd) such connections
smbdirect_listen_connect_request() rejected every new connection with
-EBUSY, so an unauthenticated peer was able to permanently stop
ksmbd from accepting SMB-Direct connections.

Now a failed child moves itself to a new listen.orphaned list at the
end of smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work(), after the disconnect was
started, and queues listen.purge_orphaned_work, which releases it
with smbdirect_socket_release(), without holding the listener's
rdma_lock_handler() lock, in the same way smbdirect_socket_destroy()
does for the remaining children. Orphaned sockets still count against
the backlog until they are released.

sc->accept.listener is now only changed under listener->listen.lock
and whoever clears it is responsible for releasing the socket:
smbdirect_socket_accept(), purge_orphaned_work or the destroy of the
listener.

In order to make that work:

- a struct smbdirect_socket that is a listener is now freed via
  kfree_rcu(), so that a child can dereference sc->accept.listener
  under rcu_read_lock(), even if the listener is released concurrently.

- smbdirect_listen_connect_request() adds nsc to the listen.pending
  list and sets nsc->accept.listener before it calls
  smbdirect_accept_connect_request(), and always returns 0 so the
  rdma_cm core keeps the connection id and nsc owns it. On a non-zero
  return it schedules nsc's teardown with
  smbdirect_socket_schedule_cleanup(), which orphans it off the
  listener so that purge_orphaned_work releases it; nsc destroys its
  own connection id with rdma_destroy_id() in that teardown. The
  teardown has to be deferred because the rdma_cm core holds nsc's
  id_priv->handler_mutex across the handler, so nsc->rdma.cm_id must
  not be destroyed synchronously from here. That same handler_mutex
  (and the listener's) also guarantees nsc can't go away under us,
  so setting the listener before the call is safe and lets a failure
  orphan nsc.

- smbdirect_accept_negotiate_recv_work() no longer moves a socket to
  the ready list if it already failed or no longer belongs to the
  listener. Every accepting socket has a listener, so if
  sc->accept.listener is already cleared, it no longer sends a
  negotiate response, as the socket is about to be released.

- smbdirect_socket_destroy() of the listener disables
  purge_orphaned_work and also releases the orphaned sockets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: serialize directory emptiness checks with readdir

SMB2 QUERY_DIRECTORY holds fp->readdir_lock while it calls iterate_dir()
on fp->filp. An SMB2 SET_INFO request with FILE_DISPOSITION_INFORMATION
can resolve the same FileId and call ksmbd_vfs_empty_dir() on the same
filp without that lock.

iterate_dir()'s inode read lock permits concurrent readers and does not
serialize per-file iterator state. ext4 stores its dx readdir cursor and
fname RB tree in file->private_data. Concurrent reset or refill can
therefore free a fname node while the other worker still traverses it or
retains its RB-tree link, resulting in use-after-free accesses.

An authenticated SMB client with list and delete rights on a directory in
a writable KSMBD share backed by ext4 can trigger this when the directory
takes the dx readdir path. The client overlaps an SMB2 QUERY_DIRECTORY
request with an SMB2 SET_INFO request carrying FILE_DISPOSITION_INFORMATION
on one live FileId.

171df27077fb, the unmodified kernel reported a cross-worker use-after-free
before a panic. The first report's access and free stacks show the two
request paths directly (trimmed):

  Read of size 8 by task kworker/2:0/29

  Call Trace:

   ext4_readdir+0x175a/0x2f40
   iterate_dir+0x1b6/0x630

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: do not pass a NULL buf to is_oplock_break()

receive_encrypted_read() sets *num_mids = 1 and never writes the
caller's bufs[]. Offload returns -1 with *num_mids = 0, so the
demultiplex thread skips the frame. The inline decrypt path
returns 0 even when smb2_find_mid() fails.

cifs_demultiplex_thread() then treats mids[i] == NULL as an
oplock break and calls is_oplock_break(bufs[i], server) with
bufs[i] still NULL. smb2_is_valid_oplock_break() reads
hdr.Command at offset 12 and oopses.

A large encrypted READ whose MessageId does not match is enough
to panic cifsd.

    Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
    0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range
    [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f]
    CPU: 0 PID: 100 Comm: cifsd
    RIP: smb2_is_valid_oplock_break+0xc8/0x2270 [cifs]
    cifs_demultiplex_thread
    Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Return -1 when inline decrypt finds no mid, and skip
is_oplock_break() plus the unknown-frame dump when bufs[i]
is NULL. receive_encrypted_standard() already assigns
bufs[*num_mids].

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: cls_flower: avoid stale mask references after delete

Flower releases a mask reference when a filter is removed from the
classifier. The filter object can remain alive while dump, walk, or
hardware reoffload paths hold a reference to it. Those paths can then
dereference f->mask after the mask has already been released.

Keep the mask reference until the filter reference count reaches zero.
Release the mask synchronously from the final __fl_put() while the caller
still holds the tcf_proto reference, and leave the existing RCU work to
free the mask. This keeps the mask available to every reader that still
holds the filter.

The filter is still removed from the classifier indexes immediately.
Therefore, a deleted filter can temporarily retain an otherwise empty
mask; fl_delete() uses the handle IDR, rather than the mask list, to
determine whether the classifier has become empty.

Failed mask assignment can leave fnew->mask as an error or borrowed
pointer without an owned mask reference. Clear it before the common
failure path so the final put cannot release an unowned reference.

This fix does not add fields, snapshots, or per-filter memory.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Drivers: hv: vmbus: Bounds check the shared ring buffer indices

In a CoCo VM the host is untrusted. Since the VMBus ring buffer read and
write indices live in shared memory, the guest has to treat both as
potentially malicious.

hv_ringbuffer_write() copies into the ring at write_index with no bounds
checking, so the host can make the guest write packet data at any offset
up to 4 GiB past the start of the ring buffer. read_index matters too:
the available space derived from both indices is the only bound on how
much is copied, and an out-of-range index can make it far larger than
the ring.

The fix is to validate both indices before use and to use the validated
snapshot instead of re-accessing. For invalid indices,
hv_ringbuffer_write() logs and returns -EIO.

One re-read of write_index is left unchecked in this patch:
hv_get_ring_bufferindices() fetches it again for the prev_indices
trailer. The value is only returned to the host and is not used as an
offset or length for indexing. Since this is not a security issue, it is
addressed later in the series.

Open-coding the bytes available arithmetic keeps the fix free of
prerequisites; a later patch refactors it into a helper function.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix OOB read and cross-share confusion in ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect()

ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect() indexes
ab_pathname[share->path_sz + 1] without checking that the path is
longer than share->path_sz + 1 (d_path() fills the buffer from the
end). A durable fp is not bound to its original share, so a client
can preserve a file from a short-path share and reconnect it on a
long-path share, making strcmp() read past the PATH_MAX buffer -
with a long enough share path this oopses the kernel, and on a
mapped page it also gives a byte-equality oracle on adjacent heap
(the reconnect succeeds exactly when the out-of-bounds string
equals the requested name). A same-share variant with the durable
fp at the share root reads 1 byte past the buffer
(strlen(ab_pathname) == share->path_sz).

Check before comparing: the path must be longer than share->path_sz,
it must start with share->path, and the next character must be '/'.
The share root itself is accepted only for an empty name.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix parent dentry lifetime in directory enumeration

ksmbd_populate_dot_dotdot_entries() builds the ".." entry from
the open directory's d_parent and passes that pointer to
ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs() without taking a reference. That pointer
is only valid while the directory stays under this parent. If a
concurrent rename moves the directory elsewhere, the old parent loses
its last reference; a following rmdir then turns it into a negative
dentry with d_inode cleared, and after the RCU grace period the dentry
itself is freed. The worker still holds the raw pointer and
dereferences d_inode through vfs_getattr() and vfs_getxattr().

A remote SMB client, authenticated or guest, triggers this by listing
a directory while that directory is moved under a new parent and the
old parent is deleted. It can be done by the client itself with write
access or by other concurrent writers, triggering null-ptr-deref and
slab-use-after-free on a KASAN build.

      [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]
  Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work
  RIP: 0010:xattr_permission+0x9d/0x160
  Call Trace:
   vfs_getxattr+0x9c/0x1b0
   ksmbd_vfs_getxattr+0x82/0x100
   ksmbd_vfs_get_dos_attrib_xattr+0x7f/0x130
   ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs+0x435/0x650

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: prevent session binding in compound requests

A failed multichannel binding can retain its target session on the work
item so that the error response can be signed. Subsequent compound
commands can then use that session together with a tree connection left
over from an earlier command.

Limit binding SESSION_SETUP requests to standalone messages during
message validation, before smb2_sess_setup() can replace work->sess.
Check both NextCommand and the current request offset to cover binding
in the first, middle and last positions of a compound. The existing
validation error path returns STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER and stops
processing the remaining commands.

This intentionally limits support for compounded binding. It is not a
protocol requirement that binding be standalone. Standalone binding and
non-binding compounds retain their existing behavior, without changing
session, tree or response encryption handling.

xprt_alloc(), reached from a write to /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy:

  CPU: 0 PID: 10404 Comm: syz.0.17 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc1-00096-gcfebfd3db73d

   <TASK>
   xprt_alloc+0x83f/0x9d0
   xs_setup_xprt+0xaf/0x3c0
   xs_setup_local+0x47/0x7f0
   xprt_create_transport+0x16c/0x730
   rpc_create+0x38e/0x7f0
   gssp_rpc_create+0xe2/0x180
   set_gssp_clnt+0xba/0x1b0
   write_gssp+0x200/0x310

   vfs_write+0x2aa/0x1050
   ksys_write+0x12a/0x250

create_use_gss_proxy_proc_entry() stores the struct net pointer as the

file descriptor does not pin the namespace either, as procfs only pins
the proc_dir_entry. write_gssp() reads that pointer back with
pde_data() and hands it to set_gssp_clnt(), which reaches xprt_init():

	xprt->xprt_net = get_net_track(net, &xprt->ns_tracker, GFP_KERNEL);

get_net_track() -> get_net() -> refcount_inc() is unconditional, so
rpc_create() assumes its caller holds a reference on args.net.
write_gssp() does not.

Dropping the last ns.count reference does not make the file go away.
__put_net() only queues cleanup_net() on a workqueue, and the
remove_proc_entry() that fences off further writes runs from the
rpcsec_gss pernet .exit method, that is, from inside cleanup_net(). A
write landing between those two points increments a refcount that is
already zero. cleanup_net() does not re-read ns.count, so the namespace
is freed anyway and the rpc_xprt -- along with the AF_LOCAL socket
opened for it -- is left pointing at freed memory. The resurrected

CONFIG_IPV6_MROUTE the same cleanup_net() worker then trips
!mr_can_free_table() in ip6mr_free_table(), which tests check_net() on
the namespace it is freeing.

reference, and then writing "1" to the still-open descriptor.

namespace is already gone. This is what procfs does for every other

and seq_open_net() returns -ENXIO when it fails. PDE_NET() cannot be
reused here because the parent directory /proc/net/rpc carries no
namespace pointer. Adding a .pre_exit to rpcsec_gss_net_ops so the
entry is removed earlier would only narrow the window, since pre_exit
also runs from cleanup_net().

Live namespaces are unaffected: a write still returns the error from
set_gssp_clnt(), a write of "2" still returns -EINVAL, and reads are
untouched.

while it is locked:

pmd sharing synchronization") the fault held i_mmap_rwsem for reading,
which everybody who zaps takes for writing.  The lock that commit
bf4916922c60 ("hugetlbfs: extend hugetlb_vma_lock to private VMAs") gave

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

accel/amdxdna: clear the mailbox channel pointer when starting it fails

aie2_create_context() allocates a mailbox channel, starts it, and on a
failed start frees it again:

	hwctx->priv->mbox_chann = xdna_mailbox_alloc_channel(ndev->mbox);
	...
	ret = xdna_mailbox_start_channel(hwctx->priv->mbox_chann, ...);
	if (ret)
		goto free_channel;
	...
free_channel:
	xdna_mailbox_free_channel(hwctx->priv->mbox_chann);

hwctx->priv->mbox_chann keeps pointing at the freed channel. That
pointer is the driver's own test for whether a hardware context has a
usable channel: aie2_destroy_context() returns early on NULL,
aie2_sched_job_run() refuses to run a job on NULL, and the message
helpers return -ENODEV on NULL. A stale pointer passes all of them.

It matters on the restart path. aie2_hwctx_restart() calls
aie2_create_context() again on a hardware context that is already live,
after aie2_hwctx_stop() has torn its channel down, and the context
survives a failure there: aie2_sched_job_timedout() discards the return
value entirely, and aie2_hwctx_resume() only propagates it. What is
left is a live hardware context holding a freed channel, and every
later user of it takes the non-NULL branch:

  - the next job submitted reaches xdna_mailbox_send_msg() on the freed
    channel, via the !mbox_chann guard in aie2_sched_job_run(),
  - a second command timeout reaches aie2_hwctx_stop() ->
    aie2_destroy_context(),
  - closing the device reaches aie2_hwctx_fini() ->
    aie2_release_resource() -> xrs_release_resource() ->
    aie2_xrs_unload() -> aie2_destroy_context(),

and aie2_destroy_context() then calls xdna_mailbox_stop_channel()
followed by xdna_mailbox_free_channel() on memory that was already
freed: a use-after-free, and a second free of the same channel.

The AIE4 management channel already does this correctly -
aie4_mailbox_start() clears ndev->aie.mgmt_chann right after freeing
it. Do the same here.

The create path itself is not affected: when aie2_xrs_load() fails,
xrs_allocate_resource() removes the solver node without calling
->unload, and aie2_hwctx_init() frees hwctx->priv, so the stale pointer
never outlives the structure holding it.

Starting a channel can fail today without this patch: the ring buffer
sizes firmware reports are rejected unless both are powers of two, and
request_irq() can fail.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: emux: Fix UAF of soundfont zones at note-on

snd_emux_note_on() looks up the matching zones via
snd_soundfont_search_zone(), which takes sflist->lock only during the
lookup and returns the raw zone pointers after releasing it.  The
caller then stores them in vp->zone without any protection.
Meanwhile, a concurrent SNDRV_EMUX_IOCTL_REMOVE_LAST_SAMPLES ioctl may
unlink and free those zones in snd_soundfont_remove_unlocked(); this
leads to a use-after-free in snd_emux_note_on(), and later at
accessing the cached vp->zone, e.g. in snd_emux_send_effect().

Fix it by holding sflist->lock in snd_emux_note_on() over the whole
zone lookup and voice setup, and let snd_soundfont_search_zone()
require the caller to hold the lock, instead.
snd_soundfont_lock_preset() takes sflist->lock for setting
presets_locked, so the removal path now syncs with the note-on finish.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/panthor: Fix TOCTOU race between GROUP_REGISTERED check and erase

panthor_group_destroy() checks the GROUP_REGISTERED mark and then calls
xa_erase() without holding the xarray lock across both. If the handle is
destroyed by another thread in between, and a concurrent GROUP_CREATE
reuses the freed ID, the first destroy erases and releases the new,
still-initializing group, leading to a use-after-free in
panthor_group_create().

Do the mark check and erase atomically under xa_lock().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

filelock: keep superblock active through delegation wait

A caller may drop its path after try_break_deleg() returns a delegated
inode but before break_deleg_wait() finishes. The extra inode reference
held in struct delegated_inode does not keep the superblock active.

After a lazy unmount, closing the delegation holder can release the last
mount reference and shut down the superblock while another task waits for
the delegation break. The waiter's final iput() can then enter the
filesystem's eviction code after its superblock-private state was freed.
This has been observed as a KASAN use-after-free in shmem_evict_inode().

When try_break_deleg() saves a delegated inode, take an active reference
to its superblock while the caller still pins the mount. Keep that
reference through break_deleg_wait() and the final iput(), then release
it with deactivate_super(). This protects every caller of the helpers,
including the mknod, mkdir, symlink and rmdir paths that drop their path
before waiting.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

fs/proc/task_mmu: pin mm_users in do_pagemap_scan()

The PAGEMAP_SCAN ioctl takes mmap_read_lock() on an mm obtained from
/proc/<pid>/pagemap without holding a reference to mm_users.

proc_mem_open() deliberately grabs only mm_count, so a consumer that
touches the address space has to call mmget_not_zero() first.  Every other
consumer in this file does -- m_start(), do_procmap_query(),
show_smaps_rollup() and pagemap_read() -- but do_pagemap_scan() does not.

Without that reference the target can reach exit_mmap() concurrently, and
exit_mmap() calls unmap_vmas() while holding mmap_lock only for reading,
which does not exclude the scanner.  For ordinary VMAs this is harmless,
as free_pgtables() and remove_vma() run afterwards under mmap_write_lock. 
A shared hugetlb VMA is different: __hugetlb_zap_end() frees the VMA's
hugetlb_vma_lock inside the read-locked phase.

walk_hugetlb_range() can therefore load vma->vm_private_data, have the
lock freed underneath it, and then down_read() a freed rw_semaphore.  The
load happens before the freeing side clears the pointer, so this is a
use-after-free and not a NULL dereference.  Any unprivileged user can
reach it with no huge pages configured, as hugetlb_reserve_pages()
allocates the lock before the VM_NORESERVE early return.

Pin mm_users across the scan, the way the other consumers do.  mmput()
from the exiting task can then no longer reach exit_mmap() while a walk is
in progress.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

fsverity: Set S_VERITY only after rollback is no longer possible

Commit f77f281b6118 ("fsverity: use a hashtable to find the
fsverity_info") changed the implementation of FS_IOC_ENABLE_VERITY to
make concurrent reads start going through fsverity verification slightly
earlier than they did before.

Instead of it happening when enable_verity() calls fsverity_set_info(),
it now happens when ->end_enable_verity() sets S_VERITY.

However, ext4 and btrfs can roll back verity after they set S_VERITY,
causing a use-after-free.

Fix that by making ext4 and btrfs set S_VERITY only after rollback is no
longer possible.  On failure, don't roll back S_VERITY, but do roll back
the filesystem-specific verity flag.

Also update enable_verity() to handle any future instances of this bug
more safely by warning and *not* freeing the fsverity_info.

Finally, tweak some comments.  Clarify one, and move information from
another to its proper place in the comment for ->end_enable_verity().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: guest_memfd: Gracefully handle xarray errors when binding a memslot

If inserting a memslot into a guest_memfd's bindings xarray fails,
propagate the error back to the caller, i.e. fail memslot creation as well.
Signalling success and continuing on with memslot creation results in
use-after-free, as the guest_memfd instance will remain reachable via the
memslot after the file is freed (kvm_gmem_release() won't nullify the file
pointer due to lack of a valid binding).

Opportunistically WARN and reject binding if KVM_MEMSLOT_GMEM_ONLY is
already set, partly to guard against goofs elsewhere, but mostly so that
KVM doesn't need to worry about clobbering flags when unwinding on failure.

Regarding the unwind, the slot must be fully prepared before inserting it
into the bindings, at which point the slot becomes reachable.  I.e. waiting
to update the slot in order to avoid the ugly unwind isn't an option.  And
as part of the unwind, explicitly nullify the relevant bindings, as xarray
can store a subset of entries when populating a range.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: pfncache: use a dedicated invalidation sequence for cache refresh

The gfn_to_pfn_cache refresh path guards against mmu notifier
invalidations which complete while it has dropped gpc->lock for the
HVA->PFN lookup: hva_to_pfn_retry() samples kvm->mmu_invalidate_seq
and retries if it changed, or if mn_active_invalidate_count is still
elevated.

That is insufficient for HVA-based caches. mmu_invalidate_seq is only
advanced by kvm_mmu_invalidate_end() when the invalidated range
overlaps a memslot, and an HVA-based cache (e.g. the Xen shared_info
page mapped with KVM_XEN_ATTR_TYPE_SHARED_INFO_HVA) need not be backed
by any memslot at all. An invalidation of the cached HVA which starts
and ends entirely within the lookup window is thus invisible to the
retry check: mn_active_invalidate_count is back to zero and the
sequence never moved. The refresh then publishes a mapping of a page
which has already been freed, and the next reader dereferences it:

  BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in kvm_xen_shared_info_init+0x3c6/0x440
  Read of size 4 at addr ffff8880599c2900 by task syz.2.383/7257

Since gfn_to_pfn_cache_invalidate_start() deliberately skips caches
which are not currently valid (including one whose refresh is in
progress, as the refresh clears the valid flag before dropping the
lock), the retry check is the only line of defence, and it must fire
for *any* invalidation, not just those hitting a memslot.

Add a dedicated kvm->gpc_invalidate_seq, incremented by every
kvm_mmu_notifier_invalidate_range_end() under mn_invalidate_lock
before mn_active_invalidate_count is decremented, and check it in
hva_to_pfn_retry() instead of mmu_invalidate_seq. Incrementing in
range_end() in the same critical section as the in-progress count
also closes the variant where the cache is activated with the
contested HVA only after invalidate_range_start() has run.

The same bug is also reachable through the per-vCPU vcpu_info cache
(KVM_XEN_VCPU_ATTR_TYPE_VCPU_INFO_HVA), where the stale mapping is
then dereferenced by kvm_setup_guest_pvclock() on the next KVM_RUN:

  BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in kvm_setup_guest_pvclock+0x5bf/0x660

This intentionally makes refresh retry on *unrelated* mmu notifier
events; restoring precision (and reworking the GPC locking more
generally) is left for a subsequent series.

Reproducers: https://david.woodhou.se/xen_shinfo_race.c
             https://david.woodhou.se/vcpu_info_race.c

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: PPC: Book3S HV: Add SRCU protection for virtual-mode HPT hcalls

The virtual-mode HPT hcall handlers (H_ENTER, H_REMOVE, H_BULK_REMOVE,
H_CLEAR_REF, H_CLEAR_MOD) call into book3s_hv_rm_mmu.c, which accesses
memslots via kvm_memslots_raw().  kvm_memslots_raw() uses
rcu_dereference_raw_check() to bypass SRCU lockdep annotation checking.
This is safe in real mode because the entire guest entry/exit is wrapped
in srcu_read_lock/unlock inside kvmppc_run_core() and
kvmhv_run_single_vcpu().

However, since commit 6165d5dd99db ("KVM: PPC: Book3S HV: add virtual
mode handlers for HPT hcalls and page faults"), these same handlers are
also executed in virtual mode via kvmppc_pseries_do_hcall(), which runs
after SRCU has already been released on guest exit.

A concurrent KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION deletion or move can therefore
call synchronize_srcu_expedited() — which does not wait for this thread —
and then kfree(slot) and vfree(slot->arch.rmap) while the hcall handler
still holds a raw pointer to the memslot.  lock_rmap() then writes to
freed vmalloc memory, leading to use-after-free and memory corruption.
Because kvm_memslots_raw() suppresses lockdep checks, this race is
entirely silent.

Fix this by factoring out the 7 HPT hcall handlers (H_REMOVE, H_ENTER,
H_READ, H_CLEAR_MOD, H_CLEAR_REF, H_PROTECT, H_BULK_REMOVE) into a
helper function, kvmppc_pseries_do_hpt_hcall(), and wrapping its call
site in srcu_read_lock(&kvm->srcu) / srcu_read_unlock(&kvm->srcu, idx).
Targeting only the HPT hcalls avoids wrapping non-HPT hcalls that sleep
(such as H_CONFER, H_REGISTER_VPA, H_PAGE_INIT) or handlers that already
acquire SRCU internally (such as H_RTAS).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: imx-jpeg: cancel timeout worker when streaming stops

Each per-fd context ctx owns a delayed_work (ctx->task_timer, callback
mxc_jpeg_device_run_timeout) armed via schedule_delayed_work() at the end
of mxc_jpeg_device_run() to recover a stalled encode/decode job. The only
existing cancellation is cancel_delayed_work() in the frame-done IRQ
handler, which de-queues a pending work item but does not wait for a
callback that has already started, and it only runs when a frame completes.

When the fd is closed while a job is in flight (the frame-done IRQ has not
fired yet), nothing syncs the worker before mxc_jpeg_release() frees ctx
with kfree() after v4l2_m2m_ctx_release(). A queued or executing
mxc_jpeg_device_run_timeout() can then recover ctx through
container_of(&ctx->task_timer) and dereference it (ctx->mxc_jpeg,
slot_data, dev_warn) after ctx has been freed.

Cancel the worker from mxc_jpeg_stop_streaming(). The cancel cannot live
in mxc_jpeg_release(): mxc_jpeg_device_run() arms the timer while holding
only hw_lock, not the mxc_jpeg->lock mutex that release holds, so a cancel
in release could still race a concurrent mxc_jpeg_device_run() that
re-arms the timer afterwards. mxc_jpeg_stop_streaming() instead runs inside
v4l2_m2m_ctx_release() -> vb2_queue_release(), i.e. after
v4l2_m2m_cancel_job() has set TRANS_ABORT and waited for any in-flight job
to finish (so __v4l2_m2m_try_queue() will not queue and v4l2_m2m_try_run()
will not run any further job for this context, which prevents
mxc_jpeg_device_run() from re-arming the timer) and before the m2m context
is freed. cancel_delayed_work_sync() removes a pending work item and waits
for a running callback, so the worker can no longer race with the
subsequent kfree(). The cancel is placed before the buffer-release loop so
a concurrently running timeout callback cannot race with it over the same
buffers. If the frame-done IRQ canceled a still-pending timer, this cancel
is a no-op; if the timeout callback has already started, it waits for the
callback to finish. The same mxc_jpeg_stop_streaming() call is also
reached from VIDIOC_STREAMOFF, which drains the worker early, although
STREAMOFF itself does not free ctx -- the use-after-free arises only
when the fd is later closed.

This bug was found by static analysis.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/rmap: don't discard lazyfree THPs at PMD level

__discard_anon_folio_pmd_locked() clears a lazyfree THP's PMD before it
determines whether the folio can be discarded, and restores it if the
folio is dirty or has extra references.  It is done under only the PMD
lock and the anon_vma read lock inside try_to_unmap_one() and no mmap lock
is held.  The temporarily none PMD causes UAF.

A parallel munmap() or mremap() is supposed to serialize with it on the
PMD lock, but zap_pmd_range() (called by munmap()) and move_page_tables()
(called by mremap()) do not take the lock when they see the temporarily
none PMD and skip the PMD.  There is no more page table walk after the
none PMD is restored:

- munmap(): free_pgtables() waits in unlink_anon_vmas() for the anon_vma
  lock, then free_pmd_range() drops the restored PMD as bad without
  removing the rmap, so the folio keeps a stale mapcount.

- whole-VMA MREMAP_DONTUNMAP: dontunmap_complete() unlinks the source VMA
  from its anon_vma while the restored PMD still maps the folio.

- plain mremap(): the THP is not moved but unmapped, so the THP's data is
  lost.

In the first two cases, the folio stays mapped, but no VMA that maps it is
linked to its anon_vma.  When the anon_vma is freed, it is still reachable
when one rmap walks the folio.  Racing lazyfree reclaim against
MREMAP_DONTUNMAP as an unprivileged user reproduces a KASAN use-after-free
in folio_lock_anon_vma_read() as reported in the Closes link.

One solution is to use an invalidated PMD instead of a cleared one until
the discard is committed, but it needs arch fixes first.
1. GUP-fast still follows an invalidated PMD on riscv, LoongArch and s390.
2. sparc64 miscounts thp_pte_count when an invalidated PMD is set again or
   cleared.

To keep the fix simple for backport, stop discarding lazyfree THPs at PMD
level instead. try_to_unmap_one() splits the PMD and discards the folio at
PTE level.

unmap_huge_pmd_locked() and __discard_anon_folio_pmd_locked() are left in
place, unused, to minimize this fix for backport and the invalidated PMD
approach is planned as a follow-up series to use them again.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/truncate: look up the end-edge straddler by index

In truncate_inode_partial_folio(), after the first split at the start
edge, folio_split() unlocks and drops the refcount of the after-split
sub-folios.  The sub-folio straddling the end of the truncation range is
therefore unlocked and only transiently ref'd in the page cache while the
code still derives it from a page pointer inside the original folio.

Between the first split finishing and page_folio() resolving split_at2,
that tail page can be reclaimed, freed and reallocated as a new large
folio in the same mapping at a different file offset.  folio2 then points
at a folio that does not cover the end boundary, yet folio2->mapping ==
folio->mapping still holds, so the stale pointer passes the mapping check
and folio_split_or_unmap() splits a folio at a wrong position (or, with a
transient refcount, a use-after-free window opens between try_get and the
split).  __folio_split()'s own folio != page_folio(split_at) check cannot
catch this either since split_at2 has been reallocated as part of the new
folio, so page_folio(split_at2) resolves back to folio2.

Look the straddler up by its page index instead.  __filemap_get_folio()
returns the folio currently covering the boundary, ref'd and locked, with
the mapping validated under the lock, so the split target is always the
real folio at the end edge.

mptcp: hold MP_JOIN msk ref when cloning reqsk

TCP request migration clones pending request sockets with
inet_reqsk_clone().  For MPTCP MP_JOIN requests this byte-copies
subflow_req->msk, but the clone does not own a reference.

The original and cloned requests can consequently drop the same msk
reference, leaving one request with a dangling pointer.  This manifests as
a KASAN slab-use-after-free in subflow_req_destructor():

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in subflow_req_destructor (net/mptcp/subflow.c:45)
  Write of size 4 at addr ff1100010e008d40 by task swapper/0/0
  CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 7.2.0-rc5-00353-gc27e36054537 #10 PREEMPT(full)

  Call Trace:
   subflow_req_destructor (net/mptcp/subflow.c:45)
   subflow_v4_req_destructor (net/mptcp/subflow.c:694)
   __reqsk_free (net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c:906)
   reqsk_timer_handler (include/net/request_sock.h:137 net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c:1147)

  Allocated by task 10014:
   sk_prot_alloc (net/core/sock.c:2246)
   sk_clone (net/core/sock.c:2488)
   mptcp_sk_clone_init (include/net/sock.h:1848 net/mptcp/protocol.c:3564)
   subflow_syn_recv_sock (net/mptcp/subflow.c:883)
   tcp_check_req (net/ipv4/tcp_minisocks.c:934)

  Freed by task 0:
   slab_free_after_rcu_debug (include/linux/kasan.h:235 mm/slub.c:2677 mm/slub.c:6439)
   rcu_core (kernel/rcu/tree.c:2645 kernel/rcu/tree.c:2897)

  Last potentially related work creation:
   kmem_cache_free (mm/slub.c:2638 mm/slub.c:6377 mm/slub.c:6504)
   __sk_destruct (net/core/sock.c:2289 net/core/sock.c:2391)
   sk_destruct (net/core/sock.c:2419)
   __sk_free (net/core/sock.c:2430)
   sk_free (net/core/sock.c:2441)
   mptcp_close (include/net/sock.h:2020 net/mptcp/protocol.c:3399)
   inet_release (net/ipv4/af_inet.c:442)

  The buggy address belongs to the cache MPTCP of size 2968
  The buggy address is 128 bytes inside a freed 2968-byte region

A non-NULL subflow_req->msk means that the request owns one reference. The
third ACK can concurrently transfer the original request reference to the
child and release it, so taking an unconditional hold on the copied pointer
is unsafe.

MPTCP sockets use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU and all current inet_reqsk_clone()
callers run in an RCU read-side critical section. Document and
lockdep-check that calling-context requirement.  Read the pointer from the
original request and acquire a reference only if it is still live.  Use
refcount_inc_not_zero_acquire() so the subsequent ownership validation
cannot be reordered before the try-get, then re-read the original request
to verify that it still owns the same msk. If either check fails, clear the
clone pointer; otherwise its normal destructor balances the new reference.
Mark the ownership-transfer store with WRITE_ONCE() to match the lockless
reads.

The following patch completes the clone fixup for MP_CAPABLE token
ownership. Both patches carry the same Fixes tag and are required for
stable backports.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: sched: prevent scheduling deactivated qdiscs

TAPRIO can schedule a deactivated qdisc after some_qdisc_is_busy() has
reported it idle.

Commit 47e8dbb6e763 ("net/sched: do not reset queues in graft operations")
made graft deactivation skip queue reset, leaving TAPRIO's timer armed.

A late callback schedules NET_TX softirq work, whose dequeue path can
race the unlocked child-queue reset in taprio_reset(). The same skb can
be queued for deferred freeing by RTNL and dequeued for transmission.
In the reproducer, the TAP reader frees it before __rtnl_unlock() reads
its next pointer. KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free in
__rtnl_unlock+0xa3/0xd0, with a read of size 8 from the freed skb.

Reject deactivated qdiscs in __netif_schedule(). Callers' RCU protection
lets the existing grace period join earlier scheduling calls before the
busy check. Restart nonempty transmit queues on reactivation so suppressed
scheduling does not strand packets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

staging: rtl8723bs: fix protected RX frame validation in decrypt path

The RX software decrypt path mishandles crafted protected frames from a
malicious AP in two ways:

1) decryptor() never checks that a protected frame is long enough to
hold the 802.11 header plus the per-cipher trailer.  All of
rtw_wep_decrypt(), rtw_tkip_decrypt() and rtw_aes_decrypt() compute

	length = hdr.len - hdrlen - iv_len;

and act on the result, and recvframe_chkmic() similarly computes

	datalen = hdr.len - hdrlen - iv_len - icv_len - 8;

for TKIP (the 8-byte Michael MIC is not accounted for in icv_len).
A frame shorter than hdrlen + iv_len + icv_len (+ 8 for TKIP) underflows
these unsigned subtractions, turning into a ~4 GiB iteration count in
aes_decipher()/arc4_crypt()/rtw_seccalctkipmic() or a ~4 GiB crc32_le()
length, causing out-of-bounds reads/writes of up to ~4 GiB starting from
the rx skb.  Reject such frames in decryptor() before touching the IV;
this covers all three ciphers and the TKIP MIC check, and also keeps the
unconditional iv[3] access within the frame.

2) validate_80211w_mgmt() keeps using the frame - two memcpys through
the stale rx_data pointer and a pkt_len update - before checking
whether decryptor() returned NULL.  On decrypt failure (e.g. a unicast
protected deauth/disassoc/action frame with a bad MIC, which this path
always software-decrypts) the skb has already been freed, so this is a
use-after-free read/write, and the caller's error path frees the frame
a second time, drifting free_recvframe_cnt.  Bail out immediately when
decryptor() fails, freeing the temporary mgmt_DATA buffer first.

Discovered by Atuin - Automated Vulnerability Discovery Engine.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mt76: mt7996: unlink TWT flow if the MCU rejects the agreement

mt7996_mac_add_twt_setup() links a new flow into dev->twt_list before
asking the MCU to add the agreement, but exits without unlinking the flow
if the request fails. The flow-ID and table masks are only committed
after MCU success, so the still-linked flow is invisible to the
mask-gated teardown paths.

If the station retries the setup, the same slot is cleared and its
embedded list node reinitialized while it is still linked, corrupting
dev->twt_list. If the station disassociates instead, teardown skips the
flow and station storage can be freed while the node remains linked. A
later scheduling or debugfs twt_stats walk can then dereference the
freed flow, resulting in a use-after-free.

list to its pre-request state while leaving the unchanged mask and
agreement accounting untouched.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ufs: use u64 for directory size in ufs_last_byte

ufs1_read_inode() and ufs2_read_inode() copy the untrusted 64-bit
on-disk size into inode->i_size.  ufs_last_byte() then truncates that
value to an unsigned int before calculating the valid extent of a
directory folio.

A directory size of exactly 4 GiB is truncated to zero.  In
ufs_find_entry(), subtracting the requested record length from that zero
forms an endpoint almost 4 GiB beyond the mapped folio.  A crafted UFS2
image produces:

  BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in ufs_find_entry+0x583/0x6e0 [ufs]
  Read of size 1
  ...
  ufs_find_entry
  ufs_inode_by_name
  ufs_lookup
  __lookup_slow
  path_lookupat

The KASAN classification reflects that the adjacent physical page was
free; the source-level operation is an out-of-folio read.  A controlled
UFS1 test with CONFIG_UFS_FS_WRITE enabled also made ufs_find_entry()
return a directory entry from an adjacent anonymous page.  unlink() then
passed that pointer to ufs_delete_entry(), which cleared the adjacent
page's 3
2-bit d_ino.  This write result reproduced three out of three
times.

UFS normally requires a privileged mount path.  A relevant boundary is
a privileged automounter or image-processing service handling an
attacker-supplied filesystem.  The write primitive additionally requires
UFS1 to be mounted read-write with CONFIG_UFS_FS_WRITE enabled; the read
is reachable with read-only UFS2.

Keep the intermediate size arithmetic at 64 bits so non-final pages are
bounded at PAGE_SIZE.  With this change, the same controlled tests reach
the real on-disk directory entry and produce no adjacent-page write or
KASAN report.  A reproducer and full validation logs are available on
request.

The vulnerable helper is present in v7.2-rc3, v7.1, v6.18.38, v6.12.95,
v6.6.111, and upstream master at 1229e2e57a5c.  Runtime reproduction and
fix validation were performed in an x86-64 QEMU guest running v7.2-rc3
with generic KASAN.

nvmet-auth: serialize access to DH-HMAC-CHAP state to fix UAF

A REPLY AUTH_SEND command can derive a dhchap_skey key while a
concurrent AUTH_RECEIVE command observing this REPLY state executes
the failure path and frees that key. The REPLY command then continues
and writes into freed memory, causing a use-after-free. KASAN reports

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: hold a lock reference across grant AST enqueue

A newly granted remote lock must remain alive until its grant AST is
queued.  dlmlock_master() publishes the lock on res->granted with its base
and queue references, then drops res->spinlock before calling
dlm_queue_ast().  The resource's reserved AST count does not retain the
lock itself.

This can fail when a peer dies with an immediately grantable CREATE
buffered on its socket.  O2NET's node-down callback flushes receive work
before DLM cleanup, but the flush only waits for work queued on entry.  A
data-ready callback that already selected the socket container can queue
new receive work after the flush advances its work color.  Socket shutdown
does not discard bytes already queued for TCP receive.

The late receive work and DLM node-down cleanup can interleave as
follows (the lock reference operations shown are before this fix):

  -----------------        ----------------         --------------
  o2net_data_ready()
    select sc under
    callback read lock
                           o2net_disconnect_node()
                             queue shutdown
                             begin flush; new color
    queue sc_rx_work
    in the new color
    release callback lock
                             shutdown socket
                             flush returns
                                                    read buffered CREATE
                                                    dlmlock_master()
                                                      lock res->spinlock
                                                      add lock to granted
                                                      unlock res->spinlock
                           DLM node-down cleanup
                             lock res->spinlock
                             dlm_free_dead_locks()
                               unlink lock
                               put queue/base refs
                               free lock
                             unlock res->spinlock
                                                    dlm_queue_ast()
                                                      __dlm_queue_ast()
                                                      read lock->lockres
                                                      (use-after-free)

DLM cleanup holds res->spinlock while dlm_free_dead_locks() drops the
queue and base references.  The CREATE handler no longer holds that
spinlock when __dlm_queue_ast() reads the lock, before taking its AST list
reference.

Take a temporary lock reference under res->spinlock when a grant AST will
be queued, and drop it after dlm_queue_ast().  This keeps the lock alive
across cleanup until the AST path has taken its own reference, without
reversing the existing AST/resource lock order.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: hold the lookup reference across convert AST enqueue

dlm_convert_lock_handler() drops the reference it took when it found the
lock on res->granted at its leave label, one statement before it calls
dlm_queue_ast().  dlm_free_dead_locks() takes res->spinlock and drops the
list and base references, so a peer death landing in that gap leaves the
handler's own put as the one that frees the lock, and __dlm_queue_ast()
then reads lock->lockres from freed memory.

The handler is registered next to dlm_create_lock_handler(), so a convert
message buffered on a dying peer's socket arrives on the same o2net
receive work that o2net_disconnect_node() does not wait for.  The two can
interleave as follows, with the reference counts as they are before this
fix:

  Socket data-ready       Node-down thread      Receive worker
  -----------------       ----------------      --------------
  o2net_data_ready()
    select sc under
    callback read lock
                          o2net_disconnect_node()
                            queue shutdown
                            begin flush; new color
    queue sc_rx_work
    in the new color
    release callback lock
                            shutdown socket
                            flush returns
                                                read buffered convert_lock
                                                dlm_convert_lock_handler()
                                                  find lock on res->granted
                                                  dlm_lock_get()  refs = 3
                                                  lock res->spinlock
                                                  __dlmconvert_master()
                                                    call_ast = 1
                                                  unlock res->spinlock
                          DLM node-down cleanup
                            lock res->spinlock
                            dlm_free_dead_locks()
                              unlink lock
                              put list ref  refs = 2
                              put base ref  refs = 1
                            unlock res->spinlock
                                                dlm_lock_put()  refs = 0
                                                  free lock
                                                dlm_queue_ast()
                                                  __dlm_queue_ast()
                                                  read lock->lockres
                                                  (use-after-free)

__dlmconvert_master() only moves the lock between lists, so the count
entering the gap is base, list and lookup.  Drop the lookup reference
after the AST is queued instead of before it and the race ends with the
one __dlm_queue_ast() took, which dlm_flush_asts() releases later with
ast_pending cleared and ast_list unlinked.  No extra get is needed, and
the normal case ends with the same count as before.

dlmconvert_master() has the same shape but is only reached from dlmlock()
for a lock this node owns, which dlm_free_dead_locks() never matches.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: fix chunk number of the first chunk in a local quota file

Mounting a crafted OCFS2 image can corrupt kernel memory.  When the
local quota file header of such an image claims zero chunks, the first
quota entry allocated during the mount gets a chunk number taken from a
kernel pointer, and releasing that entry clears a bit far outside the
chunk bitmap.

The write will corrupt the data stored at that address, and the
corruption may lead to a system crash or damage unrelated data. 
Mounting requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so it takes an untrusted image, such
as removable media or a loop mount of a file from elsewhere.

Since the chunk number comes from a kernel pointer, the address of the
bit that gets cleared differs from boot to boot, and the issue has been
reported under several titles:

- BUG: unable to handle kernel paging request in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: slab-use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KFENCE: use-after-free write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot

Note that none of these is a use-after-free in the quota code: the
chunk and its buffer head are alive.  The bit that gets cleared lies
far outside the bitmap.  KASAN and KFENCE name each report based on the
object occupying that address, which explains why the same issue is
reported under so many different titles.  In the report I sent, the
address fell in a free page, which KASAN labels use-after-free.

There are known reproducers.  Both a syzkaller and a C reproducer are
available from the Google Drive link [1] in my report thread.  The
issue was found by our modified syzkaller, not a theoretical thing
found by an LLM.  I have not seen it outside fuzzing, so it is not
affecting me in the real world.

The local quota file in OCFS2 is divided into chunks, and each chunk
begins with a header block holding a bitmap of the quota entries that
chunk has handed out.  Chunks are numbered from zero, and that number is
used to convert the file offset of an entry back into a bit position in
the bitmap.  ocfs2_local_quota_add_chunk() appends a new chunk to the
in-memory list and numbers it one past the chunk that was last:

	list_add_tail(&chunk->qc_chunk, &oinfo->dqi_chunk);
	chunk->qc_num = list_entry(chunk->qc_chunk.prev,
				   struct ocfs2_quota_chunk,
				   qc_chunk)->qc_num + 1;

The predecessor is looked up after the new chunk is added to the list, so
if the list was empty, the prev pointer is the list head itself.  The head
is the dqi_chunk member of struct ocfs2_mem_dqinfo and is not a chunk, so
reading qc_num through it lands 16 bytes past the start of the head, on
the dqi_gqinode pointer that follows it.  The first chunk of the file is
then numbered with the lower half of a kernel pointer instead of 0.

The list is empty when the local quota file header claims the file has no
chunks.  ocfs2_local_read_info() takes dqi_chunks from that header without
validating it, so an image with dqi_chunks == 0 takes this path when the
first quota entry is allocated.

ocfs2_create_local_dquot() turns the bad number into a file offset with
ol_dqblk_off(), which shifts a 32-bit block number left by the block size
bits, so the top bits of such a large block number are lost. 
ocfs2_local_release_dquot() turns the offset back into a bit index with
ol_dqblk_chunk_off(), using the full chunk number, so the lost bits push
that index far outside the bitmap, and clearing it corrupts unrelated
memory.

Compute the chunk number before putting the chunk on the list, and use 0
when the list is empty.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: pin refcount trees before dropping the lookup lock

A refcount tree returned to ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() must stay alive
until that caller releases its operation reference. However,
ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() returns the cached pointer after dropping
osb_lock, and the caller only takes its kref afterwards. The registry
reference does not protect this gap from concurrent removal.

This can happen when another node frees a refcount root and reuses its
block with a different generation while this mount retains the old
cached tree. Two local operations on different inodes sharing the new
root, such as data CoW and an external xattr update, can then look up
the same stale tree. Their inode locks are independent, and both the
REFCOUNT DLM lock and rf_sem are acquired after the first operation
reference.

The following ordering is possible, with no other operation references:

  Data CoW                         Xattr update
  --------                         ------------
  Look up the old tree under
    osb_lock, then drop osb_lock
                                   Look up the same tree and take a kref
                                   Acquire the tree locks and read the
                                     new on-disk generation
                                   Erase the old tree under osb_lock
                                   Unlock and drop the operation kref
                                   Drop the registry kref, freeing tree
  Take a kref through the
    freed tree pointer

The final kref_get() accesses freed rf_getcnt storage, and subsequent
accesses in ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() also use the freed allocation.

Take the operation reference in ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() before
releasing osb_lock, including when an insertion loses to another lookup.
Removal must acquire the same lock, so it cannot drop the registry
reference before the lookup has pinned the tree. Keep the existing
unlock and error path puts. The two callers that already hold the
refcount tree lock keep their borrowed lookup behavior and do not
acquire an extra reference.
